q: What are the five parts of a prompt written as a working brief?
options: Outcome, audience and situation, material, limits, format
Role, tone, length, keywords, examples
Goal, budget, channel, KPI, deadline
Context, tokens, attention, model, tools
explain: Write a prompt the way you'd brief a new colleague: outcome, audience and situation, material to use, limits to respect, form of a useful result.

q: Uploading a LOOP product sheet to an assistant…
options: Retrains the model on LOOP
Gives the model working information for this task only
Permanently changes the model's knowledge
Has no effect on the output
explain: Context supplies working information; model training is a separate process. Students often confuse the two.

q: An AI draft says “LOOP keeps drinks cold for 24 hours”, but the product sheet says nothing about insulation. What should the assistant do?
options: Keep the claim — it's typical for steel bottles
Remove the bottle size too, to be safe
Flag it as unsupported, ask for test data, and use only known facts
Replace it with “keeps drinks cold all day”
explain: It should flag the claim, ask for test data and propose wording limited to known facts (750 ml, steel) — not quietly keep it.

q: Which is an example of predictive (not generative) AI?
options: A first draft of an ad
An AI-generated bottle image
Estimating the likelihood of purchase
Writing a landing page
explain: Predictive estimates an outcome; generative creates an output. Real workflows often mix both.

q: Search spent €600 and drove 60 purchases. What is the CPA?
explain: CPA = spend ÷ purchases = €600 ÷ 60 = €10.00.

q: In the LOOP pilot, why does ROAS rank channels exactly as CPA does?
options: Because spend was equal per channel
Because every purchase is exactly one €29 bottle
Because retargeting has the most impressions
Because the attribution windows differ
explain: With constant order value, revenue is just purchases × €29, so revenue doesn't change the channel story.

q: Why might retargeting's strong ROAS (4.35) be misleading?
options: It reaches mostly people already interested, so attribution flatters it
It has the highest CPA
Its data is real while the rest is synthetic
It ignores the attribution window
explain: Retargeting reaches people already interested and depends on prospecting to fill its audience.

q: Noy & Zhang (Science, 2023) found that with ChatGPT on writing tasks…
options: Time rose 40%, quality fell 18%
Time fell ~40%, graded quality rose ~18%
No measurable difference
Quality doubled for every task
explain: 453 professionals; time fell about 40% and graded quality rose about 18%. Limits: specific tasks, an older model, graders didn't fact-check.

q: Why can't LOOP claim to be “the most sustainable bottle in Europe”?
options: Because it's made of steel
EU Directive 2024/825 (EmpCo) bars generic environmental claims without recognised evidence
Because LOOP only sells in Barcelona
Because the GDPR forbids it
explain: Since 27 September 2026, EmpCo bars generic environmental claims unless recognised excellent environmental performance can be shown.

q: A weekly AI campaign report needs four things. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Schedule and data source
Comparison period
Threshold for a meaningful change
A fully automated publish step
explain: The four: schedule and data source, comparison period, a threshold (e.g. CPA moves >20%), and a named reviewer.

q: Which analytics level answers “What should we do?”
options: Descriptive
Predictive
Prescriptive
Diagnostic
explain: Descriptive: what happened. Predictive: what will happen. Prescriptive: the system recommends the action.

q: What is the main risk of an AI-prepared audit or analysis?
options: It is only as good as the sources it was given, so it can be confidently wrong
It always takes longer than an analyst doing the same work by hand
It can only describe the past and never recommend an action
It refuses to answer when the data has any gaps in it
explain: AI analyses only what it is given: always check the source.

q: Which of these is something AI-powered analytics adds?
options: Automation, deeper analysis like predicted churn, and explaining what drives results
Exact data with no need for cookies or consent
A replacement for the analyst's interpretation and context
Guaranteed causes for every change in the metrics
explain: Automates (alerts, checks, reports), goes deeper (micro-segments, predictions), explains (beyond correlation).

q: What does GEO stand for?
options: Geographic engagement optimisation
Generative engine optimisation
Global e-commerce operations
Growth experiment orchestration
explain: Publishing content so generative engines (like ChatGPT) surface your brand — e.g. Euromon PLV listed first by Oct 2026.

q: Countdown timers, "personal" offers and inflated discounts used to pressure users are called…
options: Dark patterns
Micro-conversions
Dynamic pricing
Prescriptive analytics
explain: The same personalisation that helps users can be turned against them.

q: If every company can use the same AI, where does the competitive edge come from?
options: Your own data, and how much you learn from it
Using the newest AI model before competitors do
Spending more than competitors on the same tools
Keeping technology as a support function
explain: Technology is a strategic asset; your data makes you hard to copy.

q: Which guardrail responds to the risk of bias in AI models?
options: Regular audits and diverse data
Privacy by design
A human in the loop
Asking for user consent
explain: Bias → audits and diverse data; privacy → privacy by design; transparency (black box) → human in the loop.

q: Which guardrail responds to the black-box problem?
options: Regular audits
Privacy by design
A human in the loop
Diverse data
explain: Bias → audits and diverse data. Privacy → privacy by design. Transparency → a human in the loop.

q: Personalisation needs data, and GDPR demands consent. Which guardrail responds to this privacy risk?
options: Privacy by design
A human in the loop
Regular audits and diverse data
Conversational analytics
explain: The three guardrails: bias → regular audits and diverse data; privacy → privacy by design; transparency (black box) → a human in the loop.

q: Showing different images, headlines and offers to each visitor belongs to which family of AI use cases?
options: Personalisation
Productivity
Visibility
Creativity & UX
explain: Productivity = automated A/B tests and flows; visibility = programmatic ads, AI SEO; creativity & UX = generative design.

q: What are the four pillars of a CRM?
options: Strategy, data, processes, people
Sales, marketing, service, IT
Target, trigger, content, channel
Acquire, convert, grow, retain
explain: Technology + AI is the enabler that centralises, automates and anticipates — not the goal.

q: In the CRM methodology, what starts a process?
options: The target
The trigger
The content
The channel
explain: Every process has four elements: target, trigger, content, channel. The trigger is the action or event that starts it.

q: “You're running out of dog food: shall we send some?” is an example of which experience approach?
options: Reactive
Proactive
Predictive
Collaborative
explain: Predictive: AI anticipates needs not yet expressed. Proactive gets ahead of a known problem.

q: Which AI use fits the Retention stage of the lifecycle?
options: Predictive lead scoring
Next best offer
Churn prediction
Conversational agents
explain: Acquisition: lead scoring · Conversion: conversational agents · Growth: next best offer · Retention: churn prediction · Reactivation: smart campaigns.

q: Which system answers “Who is this person across all our systems?”
options: CRM
ERP
CDP
MAP
explain: A CDP unifies data from several systems into a single profile.

q: Which AI layer belongs to HubSpot?
options: Agentforce
Breeze
Copilot
Zia
explain: Salesforce → Agentforce · HubSpot → Breeze · Dynamics 365 → Copilot · Zoho → Zia.

q: Under the EU AI Act, what applies from August 2026?
options: Prohibited practices
Transparency: tell people they're talking to an AI and label generated content
High-risk systems such as credit scoring
Nothing new
explain: Feb 2025: AI literacy and prohibited practices · Aug 2026: transparency · Dec 2027: high-risk (postponed by the Digital Omnibus).

q: GDPR Article 22 gives people the right…
options: To have their data deleted
Not to be subject to solely automated decisions
To receive marketing emails
To access the source code
explain: Relevant whenever a CRM automates decisions about customers.

q: In the abandoned-cart example, what's the content rule the first time?
options: Always a 10% discount
Products and size in stock, no discount
Free shipping
A generic newsletter
explain: AI adds value by predicting who'll buy without an incentive, so no margin is given away.

q: A DMP mainly relies on…
options: First-party data in a unified hub
Anonymous third-party data, usually expiring after ~90 days
Manually entered sales notes
ERP stock data
explain: DMPs build audience segments for ads; the phase-out of third-party cookies is a challenge for them.

q: Which is listed as a common pitfall with AI-powered CDPs?
options: Starting with send-time optimisation
Scoring before resolving identities
Closing the feedback loop
Enforcing consent at the profile layer
explain: Training models on fragmented data leads to compounding errors. Other pitfalls: treating a prediction as a strategy, starting too big.

q: Which is NOT one of the three ethics questions before you automate?
options: Would the customer expect it?
Could I explain it openly?
Does it benefit them too?
Is it cheaper than a person?
explain: Trust is a CRM's most valuable asset.

q: What does a digital strategy define?
options: An organisation's priority initiatives for investing in digital technology
The channels and creative for an organisation's next digital campaigns
The technical specification for an organisation's website and apps
An organisation's targets for social media reach and engagement
explain: Its purpose is to make the business more competitive by digitalising processes and innovating business models.

q: Beyond technology, what does a digital strategy also cover?
options: Implementation: data governance, resource allocation and change management
Creative direction: brand tone, visual identity and campaign messaging
Media buying: channel budgets, bidding rules and ad scheduling
Customer service: response times, chat scripts and escalation rules
explain: Which is why it often overlaps with a digital transformation strategy.

q: How does a full digital strategy differ from a digital marketing strategy?
options: It reaches several functions: product development, supply chain and operations as well as marketing
It focuses only on technology purchases, leaving marketing and sales to other plans
It is the same thing under another name, covering marketing channels only
It covers marketing and e-commerce but excludes operations and the supply chain
explain: The goal is business effectiveness across functions, not just marketing results.

q: What is the main point of the 7Ds model?
options: Digital interactions go far beyond the website, so strategy must cover goals, audiences, devices, platforms, media, data and technology
Digital marketing has seven stages that must be completed in a fixed order, from goals to technology
Each of the seven digital channels should receive an equal share of the budget and team time
Strategy should start from the technology a company already owns and build outwards from there
explain: The 7Ds define the scope of a digital strategy.

q: In the 7Ds, "digital media" means…
options: Paid, owned and earned media channels
Mobile, desktop and IoT devices
Touchpoints such as search engines, social media and apps
Customer and operational insights
explain: Devices = mobile/desktop/IoT; platforms = search, social, apps; data = insights.

q: Search engines, social media and apps belong to which of the 7Ds?
options: Digital platforms
Digital media
Digital devices
Digital technology
explain: Platforms are the touchpoints; media are the paid, owned and earned channels on them.

q: The RACE stages Opportunity → Strategy → Action follow which planning lifecycle?
options: Situation analysis → strategy creation → implementation
Awareness → consideration → purchase
Strategy creation → implementation → situation analysis
Research → creative development → campaign review
explain: Smart Insights' RACE Growth System maps the standard strategy lifecycle.

q: What happens in the "Opportunity" stage of RACE?
options: Audit digital maturity, evaluate technology, media and data, and set baseline objectives
Review strategic options and select the priority digital initiatives to invest in
Build the tactical execution roadmap, broken into agile 90-day plans
Launch quick-win campaigns to prove the value of the digital programme
explain: Opportunity is the situation review. Selecting initiatives is Strategy; the roadmap is Action.

q: In the RACE system, what happens in the "Action" stage?
options: Build a tactical roadmap, often as agile 90-day plans
Audit current digital maturity and set baselines
Review strategic options and pick priority initiatives
Evaluate technology, media and data effectiveness
explain: Action is execution planning.

q: BCG's rule "Place big bets" means…
options: Focus on two or three high-value use cases, with short-term wins first
Spread investment evenly across many small experiments
Invest only in long transformation projects, skipping quick wins
Put the largest budget into the channel competitors use most
explain: Concentrate resources where value is highest and show early wins.

q: BCG's rule "Build new strategic muscles" is about…
options: Cultivating digital talent and internal skills
Buying more advertising inventory
Building a bigger IT department's hardware
Setting higher sales targets
explain: The five rules: assess impact, set high ambitions, place big bets, build new muscles, manage transformation actively.

q: Which SWOT quadrants are internal?
options: Strengths and weaknesses
Opportunities and threats
Strengths and opportunities
Weaknesses and threats
explain: Internal = what you control (S, W). External = the wider environment (O, T).

q: Which metric is described as the ultimate baseline UX metric?
options: Net Promoter Score
Task success rate
Time on task
Bounce rate
explain: TSR: the % of users who complete a defined task, e.g. a checkout.

q: A System Usability Scale score of 82 is…
options: Below average
Average
World class
Not possible — SUS runs 1–7
explain: Above 68 is average; above 80 is world class.

q: Why is NPS called a lagging indicator of UX quality compared to CES?
options: It measures long-term loyalty rather than the ease of a specific interaction
It is collected less often by law
It only applies to B2B
It has a 1–7 scale
explain: CES asks how easy today’s interaction was; NPS measures likelihood to recommend over time.

q: Which is an attitudinal (user feedback) metric rather than a behavioural one?
options: User error rate
Drop-off rate
Customer Effort Score
Time on task
explain: Behavioural metrics are tracked automatically; attitudinal ones come from user feedback.

q: In the CUPID score, what does the “P” stand for?
options: Performance
Pricing
Personalisation
Privacy
explain: Convenience, Understanding, Personalisation, Intimacy, Data.

q: The research says a ≈€176 upcycled jacket can't compete on price with a vintage rail. What should the boutique sell instead?
options: The design, the making and the experience
Lower prices through seasonal discounts
A wider range of second-hand vintage pieces
Fast delivery to tourists' hotels
explain: Positioning as an upcycling atelier and experience avoids the cheapest, most crowded "vintage/thrift" category.

q: How many followers did the boutique account @jackobbuczynskigarage have on 28 Oct 2026?
explain: 343 is the baseline; the proposed Oct 2027 target is 3,000. 96.9k is the main account.

q: What do the research reports identify as the main reason Barcelona Reels lost reach?
options: Poor video quality
Distribution: Polish captions reaching people who can’t visit
Instagram algorithm bans
Too many paid partnerships
explain: People who saw the September Reels engaged well (≈3.6% per view); the content reached the wrong country.

q: How many hours a week is the Gràcia boutique open, compared with nearby vintage shops?
options: 40 h vs 25 h
60 h vs 40 h
35 h vs 35 h

q: Which hashtags put the boutique in the “cheapest, most crowded category”?
options: #upcycling #designer
#vintagebarcelona #thriftbarcelona
#gracia #barcelona
#slowfashion #handmade
explain: The plan repositions it from vintage/thrift to an upcycling atelier and experience.

q: In a SWOT, a skills gap inside the team belongs in…
options: Weaknesses
Threats
Opportunities
Strengths
explain: It's internal and harmful. Threats are external.

q: A favourable trend in the market that matches your capabilities goes in…
options: Opportunities
Strengths
Threats
Weaknesses
explain: External and helpful. Strengths are internal.

q: According to the reading, where does the real value of a SWOT lie?
options: Prioritising the top 3–5 items per category and turning them into actions
Listing every possible factor so nothing is missed in any quadrant
Presenting the four quadrants as a clear visual matrix for stakeholders
Balancing the quadrants so each has the same number of items
explain: A SWOT is only useful once it drives action.

q: What is a competitive analysis?
options: Researching and documenting rivals' products, marketing and sales to sharpen your own approach
Analysing your own website's traffic, rankings and conversion rates over time
Scanning the political, economic, social and technological forces in a market
Surveying your own customers to measure satisfaction and loyalty to the brand
explain: It's external and focused on rivals.

q: Which competitor offers something different but meets the same core customer need?
options: Indirect
Direct
Aspirational
Substitute supplier
explain: Direct = same audience and similar products. Aspirational = leaders you model long-term strategy on.

q: Which competitors should be your primary focus?
options: Direct competitors
Aspirational competitors
Indirect competitors
All competitors equally
explain: Same audience, similar products: they compete for the same customers now.

q: Which are the three "surfaces" to evaluate in a competitive analysis?
options: What the brand says, what third parties say, and what AI search platforms say about it
Their products, their pricing tiers, and their sales processes
Their website, their social media and their email newsletters
Their strengths, their weaknesses and the threats they pose to you
explain: Own messaging, reviews/press/forums, and mentions in ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity.

q: Why study customer reviews of competitors?
options: Their common complaints are opportunities to win over unhappy customers
Their best reviews show which claims you should copy in your ads
Review volume is the main signal of a competitor's search ranking
Reviews reveal their prices, which change more often than their site
explain: Step 5 of the process: customer feedback and ratings.

q: How does PEST differ from SWOT?
options: PEST looks only at the external macro-environment
PEST looks only at internal resources
PEST covers internal and external factors
PEST replaces the need for a SWOT
explain: PEST = forces you can't control but must adapt to.

q: How does PEST connect to SWOT?
options: It is often the main input for the Opportunities and Threats quadrants
It is often the main input for the Strengths and Weaknesses quadrants
It replaces SWOT whenever a company enters a new country or market
It is applied after SWOT, to rank the actions SWOT has produced
explain: Both O and T are external, which is exactly what PEST scans.

q: Inflation, interest rates and disposable income fall under which PEST factor?
options: Economic
Political
Socio-cultural
Technological
explain: Economic = the wider economy's effect on purchasing power, costs and demand.

q: Labour laws, tariffs and subsidies fall under which PEST factor?
options: Political
Economic
Socio-cultural
Technological
explain: Political = government policy, law and political stability.

q: Which is NOT one of the 3 core pillars of SEO in the reading?
options: Paid search bidding
Technical eligibility (indexation)
Keyword and prompt research
High-quality, intent-driven content
explain: SEO is organic; paid bidding belongs to PPC.

q: What does "AI search optimisation" add to traditional SEO?
options: Being visible in AI-generated answers and citations as well as in search results
Using AI tools to write and publish content faster than competitors can
Paying AI platforms so they recommend your brand in their answers
Replacing keyword research with prompts typed into AI assistants
explain: SEO now covers Google/Bing results and answers from tools like ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity.

q: Why does SEO give compounding returns compared with paid ads?
options: Organic traffic builds over time instead of stopping when spend stops
Once a page reaches the top, its ranking is permanent and costs nothing
Search engines reward sites that have stopped spending on paid ads
Organic results always reach a bigger audience than any paid campaign
explain: Sustainable, long-term returns are one of the reasons SEO matters.

q: A user comparing options before buying shows which search intent?
options: Commercial
Transactional
Informational
Navigational
explain: Informational = learn; commercial = compare; navigational = find a site; transactional = act or buy.

q: A user who wants to reach one specific website shows which search intent?
options: Navigational
Informational
Commercial
Transactional
explain: The destination is already decided.

q: Roughly what share of all web searches are long-tail variations?
options: Roughly 70%
About 10–15%
About 15–20%
About 50%
explain: Head terms ~10–15%, mid-length ~15–20%, long tail ~70%.

q: Compared with head terms, long-tail keywords have…
options: Lower volume per keyword but higher conversion and less competition
Higher volume per keyword but lower conversion and more competition
Higher volume per keyword and higher conversion, but more competition
Lower volume per keyword, lower conversion and higher cost per click
explain: Fewer searches each, but visitors are much closer to buying.

q: Why do long-tail keywords usually give a better ROAS in paid search?
options: Less bidding competition means a lower CPC
Google charges a fixed lower rate for them
They always attract more clicks per impression
Their ads are shown above all other ads
explain: Lower cost per click with higher-intent visitors improves return on ad spend.

q: Why can small brands rank for long-tail keywords more easily?
options: Few websites target such specific phrases
Google gives small brands a ranking bonus
Long-tail pages don't need backlinks at all
Big brands are not allowed to target them
explain: Lower competition makes organic top positions reachable.

q: SEO improves a website's visibility in which results?
options: Organic results
Paid search ads
Shopping ads
The display network
explain: Ads and shopping are paid; SEO is about unpaid results.

q: SEO is technical work, but which two areas are central to it?
options: Content marketing and social media
Paid search and display ads
Email and SMS marketing
Print and outdoor advertising
explain: Visibility across websites, social, blogs and press depends on content.

q: What are the three steps from publishing a page to ranking?
options: Crawl → index → rank
Index → crawl → rank
Rank → crawl → index
Submit → approve → rank
explain: Bots discover the page, store it in the index, then order it for queries.

q: What happens in the "index" step?
options: The page is stored in the search engine's database of pages
Bots discover the page by following links to it
The page is ordered against others for a query
The site owner submits the page for approval
explain: Crawl = discover; index = store; rank = order in results.

q: Why do you need to know search engine market share by country?
options: The leading search engine differs between markets
Google ranks pages differently by language only
Every country uses Google
Market share sets the price of SEO
explain: Statcounter shows market share by country and period: choose engines per market.

q: A query that shows the user is ready to buy is…
options: Transactional
Informational
Navigational
Ambiguous
explain: Transactional = intent to act or purchase.

q: A query that includes a city or place shows which intent?
options: Local
Navigational
Multimedia
Informational
explain: Local searches look for something nearby or in a specific place.

q: A query with no modifier, where the engine can't tell what the user wants, is…
options: Ambiguous
Navigational
Transactional
Local
explain: A bare product name could mean buy, learn, find a store or watch a video.

q: Why look at a page's source code when doing SEO?
options: Search engines read the code, not the visual design
Users see the source before the page loads
The source code decides the page's design
Rankings depend on how short the code is
explain: On-page elements only count if they are in the HTML Google reads.

q: What is a target keyword?
options: The search term a page is meant to rank for, placed in specific parts of the page
Any word that appears most often across the whole site's pages
The brand name, repeated in the title of every page on the site
A keyword bought in Google Ads to support a page's organic ranking
explain: Placing it in title, H1, text, URL and so on is on-site optimisation.

q: The keyword principle from class is…
options: One keyword, one landing page
One keyword per website
As many keywords as possible per page
One landing page per language
explain: Each target keyword (search intent) gets its own relevant page.

q: Which on-site element is no longer a ranking factor?
options: Meta description
Title
H1
Internal linking
explain: It still affects whether people click, but not rankings.

q: In keyword selection you look for…
options: The best balance of ranking difficulty and potential traffic
The highest search volume, whatever the difficulty
The lowest difficulty, whatever the search volume
The terms competitors rank for, copied one to one
explain: High volume you can't rank for brings nothing; easy terms nobody searches bring nothing either.

q: Which is NOT a reason a page's ranking fluctuates?
options: Rankings are fixed once a page reaches position 1
You change the page's content or gain new links
Competitors change their content or gain links
The search engine updates its ranking algorithm
explain: Rankings are never permanent.

q: Which are on-site and off-site changes that cause re-indexing?
options: On-site: content changes; off-site: new links and social references
On-site: new backlinks; off-site: changes to page titles and text
On-site: competitor changes; off-site: search algorithm updates
On-site: ad spend changes; off-site: click-through rate changes
explain: Re-indexing of your own changes is one of the three causes of ranking movement.

q: According to Search Engine Journal, the top three ranking factors are…
options: High-quality content, page experience, links
Meta keywords, HTTPS, domain age
Social shares, ad spend, backlinks
Page speed, schema, sitemap
explain: New factors keep arriving, but quality content (which earns links) stays the base.

q: What does RankBrain mean for SEO?
options: You must match the search intent behind a keyword to rank
Pages are ranked mainly by how often the keyword appears
Pages are ranked mainly by their number of backlinks
Pages are ranked mainly by how recently they were published
explain: RankBrain is Google's system for understanding what searchers want.

q: If the results for a keyword are mostly informational, where should you target it?
options: In informational content such as a blog post
On a product page, to capture buyers early
On the home page, where authority is highest
In paid ads only, as it can't rank organically
explain: Match the intent the SERP shows: people are still researching, not buying.

q: When does content freshness matter most?
options: When the topic is time-sensitive, so results need updating
For every keyword equally, so update all pages weekly
Only for product pages, since prices change over time
Never: older pages always outrank newer ones in Google
explain: Freshness depends on the topic; update pages or publish new posts when it matters.

q: What do Core Web Vitals measure?
options: Real-world user experience: loading, interactivity and visual stability
Off-page authority: backlinks, linking domains and trust
On-page relevance: keywords in titles, headers and text
Index coverage: indexed, excluded and crawled pages
explain: LCP = loading, INP = interactivity, CLS = visual stability.

q: What does INP measure?
options: Interactivity
Loading performance
Visual stability
Indexation
explain: Interaction to Next Paint.

q: Why does Google penalise intrusive interstitials?
options: They block the content and create a poor user experience
They stop Google's bots from crawling the page
They hide the page's backlinks from search engines
They create duplicate content across the website
explain: Overlays (usually pop-ups) that cover the page for promotion.

q: Why is HTTPS a ranking factor?
options: The SSL/TLS certificate improves user security
It makes every page load noticeably faster
It adds the target keyword to the page URL
It earns the site extra backlinks automatically
explain: Security is part of page experience.

q: Google's algorithm updates focus on three areas. Which is one of them?
options: Moving closer to a semantic search engine
Increasing ad revenue per search
Ranking older sites higher
Reducing the number of indexed pages
explain: The three: clean spam from the SERP, adapt to user needs (e.g. mobile), become semantic (AI).

q: Google Panda mainly targeted…
options: Low-quality and duplicate content, spam and malware
Unnatural links and over-optimised anchors
Sites without a good mobile experience
Pages that still used HTTP instead of HTTPS
explain: Panda (2011) cleaned thin and spammy content. Links were Penguin's job.

q: Google Penguin targets…
options: Unnatural links and over-optimised anchor text
Low-quality and duplicate content, spam and malware
Sites whose mobile and desktop content differ
Pages slowed down by intrusive interstitials
explain: Reciprocal-link overuse, keyword-rich anchors, keyword stuffing, bought links.

q: A natural link profile is mostly made of…
options: Brand-name or non-descriptive anchor text (about 70%)
Exact-match keyword anchor text (about 70%)
Reciprocal links between partner sites (about 70%)
Footer and sidebar links from many sites (about 70%)
explain: The rest is exact or phrase match. Too many keyword anchors looks unnatural.

q: What changed in SEO because of BERT?
options: Search intent and context matter more than individual words
Exact keyword repetition became the main signal
Backlinks stopped counting as a ranking factor
Only the mobile version of pages gets ranked
explain: BERT is natural language processing: write for users, not the algorithm.

q: What does E-E-A-T stand for?
options: Experience, Expertise, Authority, Trustworthiness
Engagement, Expertise, Accuracy, Traffic
Experience, Efficiency, Authority, Timeliness
Expertise, Evidence, Accessibility, Trust
explain: Especially important for YMYL content.

q: YMYL content is…
options: Content that can affect health, money, legal or safety decisions
Content written by users rather than by the site's own experts
Content made for young audiences, held to stricter ad rules
Any page that carries advertising or affiliate links on it
explain: Your Money or Your Life: held to a higher standard.

q: What does the Helpful Content Update reward?
options: Content made for people: from real expertise, unique and valuable
Content structured to match the ranking algorithm
Long pages that repeat the keyword in every section
Pages that are republished with a new date every day
explain: User-centric content is the key.

q: The Mobile-First Index means Google…
options: Indexes and ranks the mobile version of a site
Shows search results on mobile phones only
Removes sites that have no separate mobile app
Ranks mobile apps above websites in the results
explain: Content that differs between mobile and desktop can hurt rankings.

q: Which of these stops a page from appearing in Google's index?
options: A noindex tag
A sitemap
More internal links
A canonical tag pointing to itself
explain: noindex keeps pages out and can de-index pages already indexed.

q: What is robots.txt for?
options: Telling bots which pages and files not to crawl, from the domain root
Listing every URL on the site so crawlers can discover them
Telling Google which version of duplicate pages is the master
Permanently redirecting old URLs and their authority to new ones
explain: Listing pages to discover is the sitemap's job.

q: What is a sitemap for?
options: Helping crawlers discover a site's URLs and how they relate
Telling bots which pages and files not to crawl
Passing the authority of old URLs to new ones
Marking the master version of duplicate pages
explain: Submit it in Search Console so Google crawls more often.

q: You move a site to a new domain. How do you transfer rankings and link equity?
options: 301 redirects
302 redirects
A new sitemap only
robots.txt
explain: A 301 means "moved permanently" and passes authority to the new URL.

q: What problem do canonical tags solve?
options: Duplicate or near-duplicate content on several URLs
Pages that load too slowly on mobile phones
Pages that have no backlinks pointing to them
Images that are missing their alt attributes
explain: The canonical URL is the master version Google indexes and shows.

q: Why is a flat site architecture recommended?
options: Pages that take many clicks to reach are seen as less relevant
Flat sites need no internal links between their pages
Deep pages can't be crawled by search engines at all
Flat sites can rank in more countries and languages
explain: Crawl depth (click depth) lowers perceived relevance.

q: What do rich snippets (structured data) do?
options: Help search engines understand the content and show extra info in the SERP
Make pages load faster by compressing their code and images
Hide parts of the content from crawlers to avoid duplication
Generate backlinks automatically from sites that use schema
explain: Schema.org markup; Google recommends the JSON-LD format.

q: The "halo effect" in SEO means…
options: Ranking for many long-tail keywords with one root makes the head keyword easier
A strong brand makes every page on its site rank equally well
Ranking for one head keyword makes all its long-tail variants easy
A well-designed site ranks higher because users trust it more
explain: Long-tail wins build relevance for the competitive term and its synonyms.

q: In "1 keyword → 1 landing page", the keyword should be understood as…
options: A search intent (with its synonyms)
One exact phrase, never a synonym
The brand name, used on every page
The term you also bid on in Google Ads
explain: One page per intent, with the keyword in title, H1, Hx, body, URL, images and meta description.

q: Why is content the most important element for SEO?
options: Natural backlinks and social virality are the result of high-quality content
Search engines read only the text on a page and ignore the rest of the code
Good content makes technical SEO and site structure no longer necessary
The longest page on a topic is always ranked first by search engines
explain: Quality content also brings keyword diversity and avoids duplication.

q: Link building is part of…
options: Off-page SEO
On-page SEO
Information architecture
Paid search
explain: Links from other sites are off-page factors.

q: Why should backlinks come from varied sources (forums, blogs, websites, social)?
options: Links from only one type of source don't look natural
Google only counts links that come from forums
Varied sources make the linked page load faster
It removes the need to publish your own content
explain: Natural patterns: IP variety, source variety, many domains, steady growth.

q: Which is worth more?
options: 100 links from 100 different websites
100 links from one website
They are worth the same
One footer link on a big site
explain: Link variety: diversity of linking domains matters.

q: What do search engines expect from the growth of your backlinks over time?
options: Consistent, coherent growth
Sudden spikes
No new links after launch
Growth only before algorithm updates
explain: Unnatural link growth is a signal Google watches for.

q: Why is a link from an unrelated website worth little?
options: Relevance: the context of the linking page and site matters
Links from unrelated sites are always counted as spam
Google can't crawl links between different industries
Links only count when both sites use the same CMS
explain: Valuable links come from important sites in the same industry.

q: Which link placement is most valuable?
options: In the main content, near the start
In the sidebar, visible on all pages
In the footer, repeated site-wide
In a blogroll next to other links
explain: Main content > sidebar > footer.

q: What is trust rank based on?
options: The quantity and quality of links a site receives
The age of the domain and its hosting
The size of the site's advertising budget
The number of pages the site has indexed
explain: One of the things search engines value with relevance, authority, spam and freshness.

q: Domain Authority (DA) is…
options: A Moz score (1–100) predicting ranking potential, not used by Google
A Google ranking factor shown in Search Console (1–100)
Google's own PageRank score for a domain (1–10)
A Majestic metric of a site's total traffic (1–100)
explain: Useful to compare and prioritise links; also check the traffic and the linking site's own link quality.

q: Are reciprocal links ("I link you, you link me") bad?
options: Not in themselves, but overuse hurts rankings
Always: Google penalises any of them
Never: they always help both sites
Only when the two sites share an IP
explain: Link schemes (private blog networks) are the black-hat version.

q: A Private Blog Network (A → C, C → B, B → A) is…
options: A link scheme that breaks Google's spam policy
A safe way to share links between partners
A directory of high-quality business profiles
A type of schema markup for blog articles
explain: Black-hat SEO that harms rankings.

q: What should backlink anchor text look like today?
options: Natural, like "read more" or the brand name, coherent with brand and domain
Always the exact target keyword, to show Google what the page is about
Always a bare URL, so the anchor has no keyword at all
Mostly keyword-rich phrases, with the brand name used only rarely
explain: Penguin penalised over-optimised anchors.

q: The skyscraper technique means…
options: Improving outdated popular content and telling those who linked to it
Building one very long page that targets every keyword on the site
Buying links from the highest-DA sites in the same industry
Adding a link to your site from the footer of every partner site
explain: Make the better version, then ask the linkers to point to yours.

q: Asking a site that mentions your brand to add a link is called…
options: Unlinked mentions
Broken link building
Guest posting
Image credit
explain: Turn existing brand mentions into backlinks.

q: Why analyse competitors' backlinks?
options: To find link sources, then differentiate rather than just imitate
To copy their exact link profile, one link at a time
To report their links to Google as possible spam
To lower their Domain Authority by disavowing them
explain: Better rankings come from standing out.

q: Why can newsworthy or surprising content be strong for link building?
options: Media coverage and buzz earn many natural backlinks
Google ranks news sites above all others
Press links don't count toward Penguin
It removes the need for on-page SEO
explain: The class examples all earned backlinks through PR and media attention.

q: What are the image SEO best practices from class?
options: Descriptive file name and alt text with the keyword, light file size
High-resolution files over 1 MB and the keyword repeated in alt text
Empty alt text so the image doesn't compete with the page's text
Numbered file names and images placed away from related text
explain: Aim under 100 KB, prefer .webp, alt text up to about 8 words.

q: What is the main goal of SEO measurement?
options: Track target keywords, see the impact of changes, and watch competitors
Set next month's paid search budget per keyword and campaign
Count social followers and engagement across all channels
Replace web analytics tools with a single rank-tracking tool
explain: Tools: Semrush, SE Ranking, Google Search Console.

q: Which is NOT one of the SEO metrics from class?
options: Cost per click
Organic traffic
Click-through rate in the SERP
Indexation
explain: CPC is a paid search metric.

q: Why must you verify a site before using Google Search Console?
options: GSC only gives data on sites you own
To pay for the tool
To speed up the site
To get a Domain Authority score
explain: Verify with an HTML file, meta tag, DNS record, Google Analytics or Tag Manager.

q: Which Search Console report shows why URLs are left out of the index?
options: Pages
Performance
Links
Sitemaps
explain: Indexed vs excluded URLs, with reasons such as robots.txt or noindex.

q: What does an SEO spider (crawler) tool do?
options: Crawls a site and collects each page's titles, headers and meta data
Shows search volume and CPC estimates from Google Ads
Finds and buys backlinks from high-authority websites
Writes optimised meta descriptions for every page
explain: Screaming Frog is the example; useful for audits of your own or competitors' sites.

q: In web basics, what is the role of CSS?
options: The style: colours, sizes, fonts and layout
The structure: headings, paragraphs and links
The behaviour: interaction in the browser
The storage: saving the site's data
explain: HTML = skeleton, CSS = style, JavaScript = the brain (behaviour).

q: Which language is "the skeleton" of a website?
options: HTML
CSS
JavaScript
SQL
explain: HTML defines structure and content with tags.

q: What happens after the browser sends an HTTP(S) request?
options: The server answers with files the browser then draws
The browser builds the page from its own cache only
The domain registrar sends the page to the user
The database draws the page on the screen
explain: URL → request over HTTP(S) → server returns HTML, CSS, JS, images, fonts → browser renders.

q: Which body defines the technical standards websites are built on?
options: W3C
ICANN
Red.es
Google
explain: ICANN and Red.es are about domain names, not web standards.

q: Besides HTML, CSS and JS, a modern site usually also has…
options: A framework, a backend server and a database
A second domain, a CDN and a mobile app
A CMS, a builder and a template
A sitemap, robots.txt and a canonical tag
explain: e.g. React/Next.js, Node.js or Python on the server, PostgreSQL or MySQL.

q: Which type of website is the most SEO-friendly according to the class table?
options: Blog or magazine
Web app / PWA
Platform / SaaS
Portal or intranet
explain: Blogs aim at content and rankings (very high). Web apps, SaaS and intranets score low.

q: A landing page's main goal is…
options: Immediate conversion
Branding and corporate presence
Content and rankings
Private access to internal tools
explain: Corporate site = branding; blog = rankings; intranet = internal tools.

q: Compared with the traditional model, building a corporate site with a builder + AI mainly changes…
options: Cost and time: from ≈ €12,000 and 4 months to a subscription plus a few hundred euros
Quality: AI-built sites always outrank traditionally built sites in search
Ownership: the AI provider keeps the rights to the website it generates
Nothing: each specialist role is still needed and paid as before
explain: Each role (copy, translation, design, development, QA) is replaced or helped by tools.

q: Which role turns the visual design into HTML and CSS and makes it responsive?
options: Web designer / layout developer
UI/UX designer, who owns usability and navigation
Backend developer, who owns the server logic
DevOps engineer, who owns cloud deployment
explain: UI/UX defines structure and usability; the layout developer builds it.

q: Who handles server logic, databases and APIs?
options: The backend developer
The frontend developer
The UI/UX designer
The QA tester
explain: Processes the user never sees, like authentication or data processing.

q: Which role tests for bugs and usability problems before launch?
options: QA / tester
Business analyst
Database administrator
SEO consultant
explain: QA checks the product meets quality standards.

q: What is the main idea of the "strategy" section?
options: There's no one-size-fits-all strategy, only one that fits the business model
Every business needs an online store to compete on the web
Strategy should be decided after the website has been built
The cheapest platform is always the right choice for a business
explain: Start from purpose, goals, audience and content.

q: Which four questions define a web strategy in class?
options: Purpose, website goals, target audience and content
Budget, platform, domain and hosting
Design, development, QA and deploy
Traffic, clicks, conversions and revenue
explain: Then, as a tip, ask an AI the same questions to find missed angles.

q: What does usability mean?
options: How easy a product is to use
How fast a page loads
How many users visit a site
How well a site ranks
explain: Good structure reduces frustration and increases conversions.

q: A wireframe is…
options: A low-fidelity sketch of a page's basic structure before design
The XML file that tells search engines which pages a site has
The final, high-fidelity visual design with colours and fonts
The code that connects the website to its CMS and plugins
explain: The navigation tree/sitemap defines pages; wireframes sketch each page.

q: Why does the navigation tree matter beyond usability?
options: It matters a lot for SEO
It sets the hosting price
It replaces the wireframes
It decides the domain name
explain: Which pages exist and how they connect affects how search engines read the site.

q: Which is NOT one of the professional design rules from class?
options: Use at least four typefaces for variety
Spacing in multiples of 8 px
Main CTA visible without scrolling
F- and Z-pattern reading
explain: The rule is two typefaces at most.

q: "UX isn't guessed, it's validated" refers to which key of good design?
options: User testing
Visual hierarchy
Consistency
Clarity first
explain: Measure, watch and adjust.

q: What is a CMS?
options: A Content Management System like WordPress or Drupal
A code framework like React or Next.js for apps
A drag-and-drop visual builder like Wix or Framer
A hosting control panel like cPanel or Plesk
explain: CMS = templates + plugins; builders = drag and drop; code = by hand or frameworks.

q: What is the main trade-off of visual builders (Webflow, Wix)?
options: Fast for marketing, but limited customisation
Fully custom, but slow to build
Free, but impossible to publish
Great for complex apps, but no design control
explain: Best for local businesses, simple corporate sites, portfolios and landing pages.

q: What does T2W mean in AI-first building?
options: Text to website
Template to website
Theme to WordPress
Test to web
explain: Also F2W (Figma to website) and I2W (image to website).

q: Which method fits complex web apps, custom portals and dashboards?
options: Code + AI
Visual builders + AI
AI-first only
CMS + AI
explain: AI-first fits micro-campaigns, A/B tests and MVPs; builders fit simple sites.

q: Which method fits content sites with an editorial workflow and several languages?
options: CMS + AI
Code + AI
AI-first
Visual builders + AI
explain: Blogs, news, catalogues and many-page marketing sites.

q: What is the class conclusion about AI in website creation?
options: AI can do almost everything, but it's best guided by an experienced developer
AI builders will fully replace every other method of building websites
AI adds little value to building websites beyond writing the copy
AI should only be used for testing a site, not for building it
explain: 2025: AI boosts every method. 2026: 99–100% can be AI, ideally guided by someone who understands the code.

q: What are the four steps of publishing a website, in order?
options: Domain → hosting → deploy → measurement
Hosting → domain → measurement → deploy
Deploy → domain → hosting → measurement
Design → development → QA → launch
explain: Some AI builders (e.g. v0.app) do all four at once.

q: What does hosting do?
options: Stores the site's files and makes them available online
Gives the website its address, like yourbrand.com
Puts each new version of the website live online
Tracks visits, clicks and conversions on the website
explain: Domain = address; deploy = publishing; measurement = analytics.

q: When you register a domain, what do you actually buy?
options: The right to use the name for a period, usually a year
Permanent ownership of the name, with no renewal
The hosting space where the website's files are kept
An SSL certificate that turns on HTTPS for the site
explain: Forget to renew and someone else can buy it.

q: Which is a good domain practice from class?
options: Short and easy to say, without hyphens or numbers
Long and keyword-stuffed for SEO
Hyphens between every word for clarity
Special characters like ñ for local markets
explain: Under 8 characters is ideal; avoid hyphens, numbers, doubled letters and special characters.

q: What is a deploy?
options: Publishing the site (or each update) so it's available online
Buying the domain name from a registrar such as Namecheap
Sketching the first low-fidelity wireframes of each page
Setting up GA4, Search Console and Hotjar on the site
explain: Every update to content or code is a new deploy.

q: Which tool gives heatmaps and session recordings?
options: Hotjar
Google Search Console
Google Analytics 4
Google Tag Manager
explain: GA4 = visits and behaviour; GSC = SEO and indexing.

q: What is a "routine" in website maintenance with AI?
options: A prompt with a schedule that an AI runs on its own
A weekly manual backup of the website's files
A WordPress plugin that updates other plugins
A checklist the QA team follows before launch
explain: It can research, write, check, publish or open a PR, and report.

q: Why should a website now be designed for agents as well as people?
options: AI agents browse, compare and even buy on users' behalf
Agents are the only visitors that count in GA4
Search engines no longer index pages
People no longer visit websites at all
explain: e.g. ChatGPT's browser and buying inside Google AI Mode.

q: What does website analytics do?
options: Tracks and measures relevant data on users' behaviour on the website
Designs the website's interface and its navigation flow
Ranks the website higher in search engine results
Stores the website's files and makes them available
explain: It gives the information needed to decide where to invest.

q: In Kaushik's definition, digital analytics aims to…
options: Drive continuous improvement of the online experience to achieve results
Collect as much online data as possible, in as many tools as possible
Replace qualitative research with numbers that are easier to measure
Report traffic figures to management at the end of each month
explain: Qualitative and quantitative data, plus the competition, for online and offline results.

q: What are the two advantages of analysing?
options: Making the best decision possible and measuring how the solution improves the issue
Guaranteeing good outcomes and removing the risk from every decision
Replacing the analyst's experience and removing all personal opinions
Collecting more data than competitors and building more reports
explain: "Without data, you're just another person with an opinion."

q: A good decision followed by a bad outcome is called…
options: Tough luck
Dumb luck
Failure
Success
explain: Decision quality and outcome quality are different things; bad decision + good outcome = dumb luck.

q: According to class, the usual obstacle in analytics is…
options: Processing raw data into meaningful insights
Not having enough data available to analyse
The high cost of the main analytics tools
Users refusing to accept tracking on websites
explain: Data → information → analytics → insights.

q: Why is the real impact of AI as a traffic source underestimated in GA4?
options: AI Overviews arrive as organic and zero-click AI answers aren't seen
GA4 blocks every visit that comes from an AI assistant's links
AI visits are first counted twice and then removed from reports
GA4 has no channel at all for traffic from AI assistants
explain: GA4 does have an AI Assistant channel (ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude).

q: Quantitative analytics measures… and qualitative analytics measures…
options: What happened / why it happened
Why it happened / what happened
Traffic / revenue
Past results / future results
explain: Numbers vs reasons.

q: Which is a qualitative analytics method?
options: Usability study
Session count
Click count
Purchase count
explain: Also questionnaires, focus groups, heatmaps, interviews.

q: What does the "fable of the blind men" teach about analytics?
options: A number needs context and the big picture to mean anything
Qualitative data is always more reliable than numbers
More data always leads to better business decisions
Only one metric really matters for each website
explain: "I sold 100 shoes" — good or bad? You can't tell without context.

q: Which qualitative tool should you always start with?
options: Content rating
Interviews
Group events
Offline survey
explain: Low time and cost, thousands of people, continuous.

q: What does an analytics maturity model describe?
options: How advanced a company's analytics is, given its needs, data and processes
How old the company's analytics tools and installations are
How many analysts and data engineers a company employs
How long GA4 keeps a company's data before deleting it
explain: The plan depends on maturity and business model.

q: What must exist before implementing tools and reports?
options: An action plan: what to measure, how and why
A finished dashboard in Looker Studio
A complete GA4 and GTM installation
A list of the tools competitors use
explain: The 8-step website analytics plan.

q: Which step comes first in the 8-step analytics plan?
options: Business model know-how
Goals (SMART)
Tools (GA4, GTM)
Metrics and KPIs
explain: Business model know-how → know the business → goals → metrics and KPIs → tools → reporting → optimisation → learning.

q: Which steps of the plan need technical rather than business knowledge?
options: Tools and reporting
Goals and KPIs
Optimisation and learning
Know the business and business model
explain: The rest rely on business knowledge.

q: Goals in an analytics plan should follow which rule?
options: SMART
RACE
SWOT
PEST
explain: Then business goals are broken into website goals and measurable micro-goals.

q: What is a KPI?
options: A metric that tells us whether the website's objectives are being met
Any number that GA4 can show in its standard reports
A business goal written out as a short sentence
A tool used to collect data from the website
explain: Each area needs its own KPIs according to its objectives.

q: What is a micro-conversion?
options: An action that brings the user closer to the main conversion
A conversion worth less than a set amount, like €10
A conversion completed on a mobile device
A conversion that GA4 cannot measure directly
explain: e.g. registering in a checkout or requesting a quote; the conversion is the purchase.

q: Which is a conversion rather than a micro-conversion?
options: A purchase
Adding a product to the cart
Requesting an online quote
Registering during checkout
explain: Conversions have a direct positive impact on company goals.

q: What makes a good report?
options: Automated as far as possible and built for its audience
As many metrics as possible, for every team
Updated by hand each day, so it's always checked
The same layout and KPIs for every audience
explain: It shows the business evolution and drives decisions.

q: What is the most common mistake after reporting?
options: Not taking action on the report's insights
Sharing the report with too many people
Including too few metrics in the report
Building the report as an automated dashboard
explain: Step 7 is optimisation: act on the decisions.

q: How should AI be used on an analytics plan?
options: To critique your plan, while you decide which changes to accept
To write the whole plan, since it knows more KPIs than you
To replace GA4 for measuring the plan's KPIs
Not at all, because AI answers contain mistakes
explain: Ask it to find unmeasurable KPIs, goals not linked to the business, and vanity metrics.

q: How is GEO different from SEO?
options: GEO asks whether AI assistants recommend you; SEO whether you show in Google's results
GEO is SEO for local businesses, focused on Google Maps listings
GEO measures paid ads that appear inside AI assistants' answers
They are the same discipline under a newer, AI-era name
explain: Measure with mentions, citations, AI Assistant traffic and share of voice.

q: In AI visibility, "share of voice" means…
options: The % of AI answers where you appear vs competitors
The number of links pointing to your site
Your share of total website traffic
How often your brand is searched on Google
explain: Mentions = brand appears; citations = they link to you.

q: What are the three main characteristics of GA4?
options: Based on events, depends on cookies, cross-device and cross-platform
Based on sessions, cookie-free, desktop only
Paid licence, server-side, single device
Based on pageviews, fingerprinting, web only
explain: GA4 measures interactions as events.

q: Why use Google Tag Manager alongside GA4?
options: Some relevant information can't be measured in GA4 directly
GA4 can't measure page views without GTM
GTM replaces the need to install GA4 at all
GTM is required to create a GA4 account
explain: Most KPIs can be measured in GA4, but not all.

q: In GA4, what is an event?
options: A unique action at a specific time, associated with a user
A visit that lasts longer than ten seconds
A report that GA4 runs on a set schedule
A group of users who share the same behaviour
explain: Page views, product clicks and add to carts are events.

q: session_start and first_visit are which type of event?
options: Automatically collected
Recommended events (predefined by Google)
Custom events (defined by you)
Key events (marked as conversions)
explain: Recommended events have a name and parameters predefined by Google; custom ones you define.

q: What is the difference between an event and a parameter?
options: The event counts how often something happens; the parameter adds detail about it
The event is used for websites, the parameter for apps only
The parameter counts actions; the event adds detail about them
They are two names for the same thing in different GA versions
explain: view_search_results counts searches; search_term says what was searched.

q: Before publishing a new GA4 event, you should…
options: Prefer recommended events and check it in DebugView
Create a custom name for every event
Publish first and check the data next month
Ask AI to confirm it works
explain: Validate every event before it goes live.

q: What is the first step of GA4 data acquisition?
options: The user accepts cookies
GA4 builds a report
GTM fires a tag
The analyst writes a query
explain: Accept cookies → JavaScript layer collects data → data reaches GA4 → analyse and plot.

q: Which statement about GA4 data is correct?
options: It's an approximation, not an exact count
It counts every visitor exactly
It counts people, not browsers
It works without cookies or JavaScript
explain: Rejected cookies aren't counted, and by default it measures browsers.

q: By default, what does GA4 measure?
options: Browsers, not people
People, not browsers
Devices, not sessions
Accounts, not cookies
explain: Cookies identify unique browsers; GA4 can be configured to join a user's devices.

q: What happens to traffic when a user rejects cookies?
options: It isn't counted
It's counted twice
It's counted as organic
It's counted as direct
explain: One reason GA4 data is an approximation.

q: 3rd-party cookies are mainly used for…
options: Analytics, retargeting and marketing
The website's own user experience
Storing the site's files
Securing the site with HTTPS
explain: 1st-party cookies serve the user experience on the site.

q: What is Google Tag Manager?
options: A tag management tool to set up measurement without going through IT
A reporting tool that replaces GA4's standard reports
A hosting service that stores a website's files online
An AI assistant inside GA4 that answers questions
explain: It handles GA4 events, ad pixels and tools like Hotjar.

q: Which of these is one of GTM's 6 fundamental elements?
options: Triggers
Dashboards
Audiences
Cohorts
explain: Accounts, containers, tags, triggers, variables, data layers.

q: Why does every GA4 metric need a comparison or date range?
options: A metric needs context to be understood
GA4 can't show a metric on its own
Comparisons make the data exact
Filters remove the bots
explain: Compare periods or segments to know whether a number is good or bad.

q: The Realtime report shows activity for the last…
options: 30 minutes
24 hours
7 days
5 minutes
explain: Realtime overview and Realtime pages.

q: Which GA4 report group shows where users come from?
options: Acquisition
Engagement
Monetisation
Retention
explain: User acquisition and traffic acquisition.

q: Under last-click attribution, which touchpoint gets the credit?
options: The last one before the conversion, with 100%
The first touchpoint of the journey, with 100%
Every touchpoint in the journey, in equal parts
The last Google paid ad in the journey, with 100%
explain: Last click on Google paid channels gives it to the last Google ad.

q: What does the data-driven attribution model do?
options: Splits credit across touchpoints by their measured contribution
Gives all the credit to the first touchpoint in the journey
Gives all the credit to the last Google paid ad clicked
Gives exactly the same credit to every touchpoint
explain: Unlike last click, every touchpoint can get a share.

q: Which Explore technique shows user journeys as a tree chart?
options: Path exploration
Segment overlay
Cohort exploration
User explorer
explain: Segment overlay uses Venn diagrams; cohort follows groups over time.

q: Which Explore technique shows how user segments relate using Venn diagrams?
options: Segment overlay
Path exploration
Funnel exploration
Blank
explain: Funnels show the journey to a conversion.

q: In an Explore, what goes in rows/columns and what goes in values?
options: Dimensions in rows/columns, metrics in values
Metrics in rows/columns, dimensions in values
Segments in values, filters in rows
Dates in rows, users in values
explain: Configuration area on the left, visualisation area on the right.

q: What is Analytics Advisor in GA4?
